passage: After her father fell ill last spring, Trisha, twenty-one, found herself running the family's grocery shop in the small town, while still finishing her BCom. Every evening she sat at the counter with the ledger, the bank loan letter, her little sister's school fee receipt and a list of suppliers to pay. One night she opened the ledger, stared at the columns and felt her whole body go still. The numbers blurred. A customer asked for sugar twice before she heard him. After closing, she sat on the step outside, not moving, while the street dogs settled down for the night. Her mother came out, sat beside her and said nothing for a while. Then: "Tomorrow, I'll handle the suppliers. You do only the bank." Trisha leaned against her shoulder.

qa.q: What did the customer ask Trisha for twice?
qa.a: Sugar.

qa.q: What does Trisha's stillness at the counter suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was flooded by too many adult duties at once, so overwhelmed that she froze and couldn't take in what was around her.

qa.q: How did her mother's offer help, and what could come next?
qa.a: Splitting the tasks gave Trisha one clear job; next they could make a shared weekly plan so she isn't carrying everything alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Trisha's mother to see her daughter frozen on the step?
qa.a: She seems to understand without words and chooses quiet presence and practical help over questions.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a small town paralysed by a sudden load of permanent family responsibilities.

passage: In her first month living alone in Stockholm, Hana, twenty-two, stood in the supermarket unable to choose between two bags of rice. That morning she'd opened three letters: a tax registration form, a notice about her apartment lease, and a reminder about her work contract. Each needed something she didn't understand. Now even rice felt like a decision too big to make. She left the basket in the aisle and walked out. At home, she lay on the floor. Her friend Anders came by with cinnamon buns and found the letters on the table. "Okay," he said, spreading them out. "Which one has a date on it?" Only one did. They filled that form together. Hana cried a little, laughing at herself. "I couldn't even pick rice."

qa.q: How many letters did Hana open that morning?
qa.a: Three letters.

qa.q: Why could Hana not choose between the two bags of rice?
qa.a: She was so flooded by the unfamiliar adult tasks in the letters that even a small choice felt too heavy.

qa.q: What did Anders do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: He sorted the letters by which had a deadline, so Hana could focus on one task instead of all of them.

qa.q: How might Anders feel finding his friend on the floor?
qa.a: He is probably worried but calm, choosing practical help and company rather than making her feel foolish.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad feeling paralysed by a sudden flood of adult paperwork and responsibilities.

passage: At the bank branch, Binita, twenty-two, sat holding a folder of forms: new salary account, tax declaration, nominee details, and the rent agreement her landlord wanted notarised by Friday. Two weeks ago she had been a student whose biggest worry was a viva. Now the clerk, Noor, was asking for a cancelled cheque, and Binita realised she didn't have a chequebook and couldn't remember whether her ID proof was the original or a copy. Her eyes stung. She stared at the forms and couldn't read a single line. 'Are you okay, beta?' Noor asked. 'I don't know where to start,' Binita whispered. Noor took the folder and made three piles. 'Today, only this one. The others can wait till Monday.' Binita breathed out for what felt like the first time that morning.

qa.q: By when did the landlord want the rent agreement notarised?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: Why couldn't Binita read a single line of the forms?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed by so many new adult tasks at once, and her mind froze.

qa.q: Why did Noor's three piles help?
qa.a: They broke a flood of tasks into one manageable step for today, which unfroze Binita.

qa.q: How might Noor have seen Binita's situation?
qa.a: As a young person facing many adult tasks for the first time, which Noor met with patience rather than irritation.

grounding: Shows a young adult frozen by a sudden pile of permanent adult responsibilities, and being helped to take one step.

passage:
Dear Tejas Bhaiya,
Sorry I didn't reply for two weeks. Since Papa's transfer, it's been me at home with Dadi, plus the new job, plus the electricity bill, the gas booking, Dadi's appointments, the house help's salary. Every morning I wake up and the list is just there, sitting on my chest. Yesterday I stood in the kitchen for twenty minutes holding the gas booking slip, not doing anything, and then cried because the milk boiled over. I know people do this every day. I just didn't know it all arrives at once and never leaves. I'm writing because you said to tell you if it got too much. It's too much, a bit. Can we talk on Sunday? I'll make a list of what I actually need help with.
Mehak

qa.q: How long did Mehak stand in the kitchen holding the gas booking slip?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Mehak mean by the list 'sitting on my chest'?
qa.a: Mehak feels weighed down and anxious from the moment of waking by all the new responsibilities.

qa.q: What makes Mehak's plan to talk on Sunday a good step?
qa.a: Mehak is reaching out instead of hiding it, and planning to name specific needs so the help can be practical.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Concerned for Mehak, but glad Mehak trusted him and told him, as he had asked. 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a young adult paralysed by a sudden load of household and work responsibilities, and reaching out.

passage: Suraj, you asked why I disappeared for a month. I'm Disha, twenty-two, and when my father had his surgery in March, everything fell on me at once. The hospital forms, the electricity bill, my little brother's school fees, my own job. I'd sit at the table with a pile of papers and just stare. I couldn't start anything. One night I cried in the bathroom for an hour. The next morning, my manager noticed and asked if I was okay. I told her. She gave me two days off, and my aunt came to stay. We made a list together and split it. It's still a lot, but I'm moving again.

qa.q: Who noticed Disha was struggling at work?
qa.a: Her manager.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling while staring at the pile of papers?
qa.a: Disha felt overwhelmed and paralysed, flooded by the sudden weight of responsibilities.

qa.q: What turned things around for Disha?
qa.a: Telling the manager, accepting help from an aunt and splitting the tasks into a list.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel hearing why Disha disappeared?
qa.a: Concerned and sorry, and glad Disha finally shared it.

grounding: Shows a young adult flooded by sudden family responsibilities and finding a way forward with help.

passage: I'm Gurpreet, and I share a flat with my cousin Baljeet. Last week I found him sitting on the kitchen floor, papers all around him: the rent agreement, a tax form, a gas connection letter, his new job's joining documents. He wasn't doing anything, just staring. "I don't even know which one to start," he said. He's twenty-one, and until last month his parents handled all of this. I sat down next to him. We sorted everything into three piles: this week, this month, later. He picked up the top paper from the first pile. It took him ten minutes. Then he picked up the next.

qa.q: How many piles did they sort the papers into?
qa.a: Three piles: this week, this month, later.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling while staring at the papers?
qa.a: He was probably overwhelmed and frozen by so many new responsibilities at once.

qa.q: Why did sorting into piles help Baljeet?
qa.a: It broke the flood into smaller steps, so he could start with one clear task.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Baljeet's situation?
qa.a: Gurpreet understands it's new for him and chooses to help rather than judge.

grounding: Shows a young adult paralysed by sudden adult paperwork and a cousin helping him break it down.

passage: Monday: Lakshmi, twenty-two, started a new job, moved into her first flat and received her first education-loan statement, all in one week. By evening she hadn't unpacked a single box. She ate biscuits for dinner and lay awake. Thursday: her manager, Shalini, noticed her rereading the same email three times. "First week everything?" Lakshmi nodded, eyes stinging. Shalini said, "Write everything down tonight. Circle three things only." The next Monday: Lakshmi had unpacked the kitchen, set up a loan reminder after calling the bank, and circled three new things. It was still a lot. But it had edges now.

qa.q: What did Shalini tell Lakshmi to circle?
qa.a: Three things only.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling as she lay awake on Monday?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and anxious, flooded by too many new responsibilities at once.

qa.q: What small step helped Lakshmi move again?
qa.a: Writing everything down and focusing on three things, so the tasks felt manageable.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel seeing Lakshmi a week later?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased that her simple advice helped.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from paralysis to action amid a sudden rush of adult responsibilities.

passage: Alka Bua sat with Naveen on the steps. "You're drowning with your first job, na? When I was twenty-one, your grandfather had his stroke. Overnight I had to handle everything: the hospital bills, the bank, my new job, your Dadi's medicines, the house. One evening I sat on the hospital bench with a pile of forms and couldn't move. I just stared. A nurse, Sister Mary, sat next to me. 'One form,' she said. 'Just the top one.' I filled it. Then the next. Then I called my cousin and asked her to handle the bank. It took me weeks to feel like a person again. But I learned: when everything comes at once, you don't carry it all at once." Naveen let out a long breath.

qa.q: Who sat next to young Alka on the hospital bench?
qa.a: Sister Mary, a nurse.

qa.q: How did young Alka feel on the hospital bench with the pile of forms?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and paralysed, unable to move.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Alka's story?
qa.a: Sister Mary telling her to do just the top form, and then young Alka asking her cousin for help with the bank.

qa.q: How might Sister Mary have seen young Alka that evening?
qa.a: She likely saw a frightened young woman frozen by too much, and wanted to help her take one small step.

grounding: An aunt tells Naveen how, at twenty-one, she was flooded by sudden adult responsibilities and began coping one step at a time.

passage: It was Monday, 9 p.m., and Jahnavi, twenty-two, had three weeks at her first job, rent due tomorrow, and her mother's insurance forms that had to reach the hospital by noon. Then her phone died. She sat on her floor in the Kolkata flat, laptop open, cursor blinking, and couldn't type a single word. Her friend Ojas knocked with a charger. He found her staring at the wall. "Talk." "It's everything," she said. "I don't even know where to start." He sat down, took a paper, and wrote three lines: rent, forms, sleep. "Rent first. Five minutes." She did it. "Forms: call the hospital helpdesk at nine tomorrow and ask what's missing." She nodded, breathing easier. "Sleep. Now." She laughed shakily. "Okay."

qa.q: By what time did the insurance forms have to reach the hospital?
qa.a: By noon.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she couldn't type a single word?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and frozen, flooded by too many responsibilities at once.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that helped?
qa.a: He broke everything into three small steps, starting with the quickest, and suggested asking the hospital helpdesk.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt finding Jahnavi staring at the wall?
qa.a: He was probably worried about her and wanted to help calmly.

grounding: A young woman is overwhelmed by work, rent and a parent's insurance forms, and a friend helps her break it down.

passage: Arohi, twenty-one, had been in Gurugram for two weeks. On her laptop were seven open tabs: rent agreement, tax declaration form from HR, health insurance choices, an electricity connection request, her bank's new account page. She sat staring at them for an hour on Sunday, not clicking anything. Her chest felt tight. Her flatmate Amandeep came in with chai. "You've been frozen like that since lunch." "I don't know what any of this means. Mumma always did this." Amandeep sat beside her. "Close everything except one." Arohi closed six tabs. "Rent agreement. Read it with me. The tax one, we'll ask HR on Monday." Arohi breathed out. "I thought adults just knew." Amandeep laughed. "Nobody knows. We ask."

qa.q: How many tabs were open on Arohi's laptop?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling as she stared at the tabs for an hour?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and anxious, paralysed by unfamiliar adult tasks.

qa.q: What approach helped Arohi get unstuck?
qa.a: Closing all but one tab, reading the rent agreement together and saving the tax question for HR.

qa.q: How does Amandeep see Arohi's struggle?
qa.a: Amandeep sees it as normal, reassuring her that nobody just knows and everyone asks.

grounding: A young woman in her first job freezes before a flood of adult paperwork until her flatmate helps her take one task at a time.

passage:
"Tanvir, you haven't eaten," Leela said, standing in the doorway of his room.
"I will. After the form."
"Which form?"
"The tax form. And the landlord's agreement. And the health insurance thing from office. And Abbu's bank papers, since he can't read small print anymore." He pushed a pile across the desk. "It all came this week. I don't know where to start. I keep opening one and closing it."
Leela sat down on the bed. "Okay. Which one has the nearest deadline?"
"The landlord's. Friday."
"Then that's tonight. Just that."
"And the rest?"
"We make a list. One a day. Your office's HR can explain the insurance. Abbu's bank has a help desk."
Tanvir let out a long breath. "I thought I was supposed to know all this."
"Nobody knows. People just start."

qa.q: Which form has the nearest deadline?
qa.a: The landlord's agreement, due Friday.

qa.q: How is Tanvir feeling about the pile of papers?
qa.a: He feels overwhelmed and stuck, opening and closing forms without knowing where to start.

qa.q: What approach does Leela suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Start with the nearest deadline and do one a day, asking HR and the bank's help desk for the hard parts.

qa.q: How might Leela feel seeing Tanvir skip meals over forms?
qa.a: Leela seems concerned and caring, stepping in calmly to break it down for him.

grounding: Shows a young adult frozen by a sudden pile of adult responsibilities and a friend's help.

passage:
The month my father got sick, everything landed on me at once. I'm Aparna, the older daughter, twenty-one, three months into my first job.
Suddenly I was the one talking to doctors, paying the electricity bill, filling his insurance claim, and answering my younger brother's school emails. I'd sit at my laptop at midnight and stare, not typing anything. I'd forget to eat.
My friend Charu came over one night and found me crying into a pile of receipts. She didn't try to fix it. She made tea, took out a notebook and said, "Tell me everything, and I'll write."
We made a list. We split it into this week, this month, later. I called my aunt for help with the hospital.
I still get flooded. But now I know where to start.

qa.q: How long had Aparna been in the first job?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel sitting at the laptop at midnight?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and frozen, staring without typing and forgetting to eat.

qa.q: What made Charu's help effective?
qa.a: She listened without fixing, then wrote everything down and split it into this week, this month and later.

qa.q: How might Aparna's younger brother be affected during that month?
qa.a: He may have felt worried about their father and relied on his sister more than usual.

grounding: A young adult recalls being flooded by sudden adult responsibilities and a friend's practical help.

passage:
Office mentor's note, first-year analysts
Jomon joined our team in July. By September, he had missed two deadlines and stopped speaking in meetings. His teammate Yash mentioned that Jomon had also just moved into his first flat and was handling rent, cooking and a parent's hospital visits for the first time.
When I met him, he said, "Every day there's something new I'm supposed to know how to do. I just freeze."
I did not give him more tasks. We sat and listed everything, work and home. We removed two lower-priority projects for a month. I also shared the company's employee support line and suggested he use it if the pressure keeps building.
Yash offered to pair with him on Mondays.
We will check in weekly.

qa.q: When did Jomon join the team?
qa.a: In July.

qa.q: How was Jomon feeling when he spoke to the mentor?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and paralysed, saying he just freezes when faced with new things.

qa.q: Which steps by the mentor helped, and why?
qa.a: Listing everything, removing two lower-priority projects, and sharing the support line eased the load and gave him help.

qa.q: How might Yash see Jomon's struggle?
qa.a: Yash seems concerned and understanding, noticing what Jomon is carrying and offering to pair with him.

grounding: A mentor records a young employee overwhelmed by sudden adult duties and the support offered.

passage:
Diary, Sunday night
I've been staring at the same pile for two hours. Lease renewal due Friday. The HR form about my provident fund. A letter about Papa's health insurance that now needs my signature, since I'm the only one of us in Mohali. The gas cylinder booking. My first project deadline at work. Every time I pick one up, the others scream louder, and I put it down again. I actually lay on the floor for a while. Tejas came over with rajma-chawal and didn't lecture me. He just made me write each thing on a sticky note and put them in order of date. Five notes. Only one was due tomorrow: the gas booking. I did it in four minutes. The rest I'll ask HR and Papa's insurance agent about on Monday.
Gurleen

qa.q: How many sticky notes did Gurleen end up with?
qa.a: Five notes.

qa.q: How was Gurleen feeling while staring at the pile?
qa.a: Gurleen felt overwhelmed and stuck, so flooded by everything at once that nothing got done.

qa.q: Why did Tejas's sticky-note method help?
qa.a: Putting each task on its own note and ordering by date showed that only one was urgent, which broke the freeze and let Gurleen act.

qa.q: How does Tejas support Gurleen without taking over?
qa.a: Tejas brings food, doesn't lecture, and just helps sort the tasks, leaving Gurleen to do them.
